# Bhaddekaratta Sutta (MN 131 (PTS MN iii 187))

**ID:** MN 131 (PTS MN iii 187)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Bhaddekaratta Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** One Fine Night
**PTS:** MN iii 187
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn131
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bhaddekaratta Sutta* (MN 131) is the opening discourse of a group of four consecutive *Bhaddekaratta* suttas located in the *Vibhaṅgavagga* of the *Uparipaṇṇāsa* in the *Majjhimanikāya* [SuttaCentral; Holz 2009; Skilling 2001]. The sutta begins with a summary (*uddesa*) consisting of a concise set of verses urging the practitioner not to revive the past, build hopes on the future, or become embroiled in the present, but rather to see things as they are and cultivate insight with present effort [SuttaCentral; Rogell 2003]. The Buddha then provides a detailed exposition (*vibhaṅga*) explaining these verses through the framework of the five aggregates (*khandha*), demonstrating that reviving the past or yearning for the future consists in finding delight in one's aggregates, whereas one avoids being bound up in the present by not identifying the five aggregates as self [Rogell 2003; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. Traditional commentary interprets the enigmatic title term *bhaddekaratta* as "one who is happy [auspicious] for one single night" (*bhaddakassa ekarattassa*) owing to insight, reflected also in Chinese renderings meaning "a good night" (*shanye*), while modern translators have rendered it as "An Exposition of the Bhaddekaratta Sutta / Ideal Solitude" and "Knowing the Better Way to Live Alone" [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Ñāṇananda 1973; Thich Nhat Hanh 1998].

Unlike most chapters of the *Majjhimanikāya*, which contain ten discourses, the *Vibhaṅgavagga* contains twelve suttas; it has been hypothesized that MN 131 was an addition to this chapter after it had already been formed in the typical ten-discourse structure [Holz 2009]. SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus identify direct internal parallels in the three subsequent discourses sharing the same verses and analytical themes: the *Ānandabhaddekaratta Sutta* (MN 132), the *Mahākaccānabhaddekaratta Sutta* (MN 133), and the *Lomasakaṅgiyabhaddekaratta Sutta* (MN 134), as well as thematic overlap with the *Mūgapakkhajātaka* (Ja 538) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also records extensive text reuse with the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), the *Diṭṭhikathā* of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga*, and the *Cūḷavedalla Sutta* (MN 44) [DharmaNexus]. External parallels identified by SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus include a Sanskrit *Sagāthāvarga* discourse, a Sanskrit fragment (SHT sutta 21) which preserves the verses followed by *dhāraṇī* formulas, Tibetan recensions such as the *Ārya-bhadrakarātrī-nāma-sūtra* (D 313), and Chinese translations in the *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26, discourse 43) and an individual translation (T 77) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Holz 2009].
